sections.overview: Bicknell’s Thrush is a small migratory songbird that breeds in northeastern North America and winters in the Greater Antilles.
sections.identification: It closely resembles the Gray-cheeked Thrush C. minimus, but tends to have a redder tail, a shorter yellower bill and a rising song ending.
sections.habitat: Breeding habitat is dense, often high-elevation balsam-fir forest, while winter habitat is moist montane broadleaf forest in the Caribbean.
sections.diet: It eats insects and other small invertebrates during the breeding season and also takes fruit, particularly outside breeding.
sections.behavior: Its secretive habits and remote breeding habitat make population monitoring difficult; females defend winter territories in dense vegetation.
sections.reproduction: At breeding sites, females may receive provisioning help from several males, an unusual polygynandrous mating system among thrushes.
sections.ecology: It was long treated as a subspecies of the Gray-cheeked Thrush before being recognized as a distinct species; the two remain close relatives and look-alikes.
sections.conservation: It is listed as Threatened in Canada and Vulnerable globally; habitat alteration on breeding and Caribbean wintering grounds and climate change are concerns.
